title: U.S. Border Officers Are Searching More Phones and Laptops
summary:
U.S. border officers are checking more travelers' phones and laptops than ever before, according to government numbers obtained by the Canadian news outlet CBC News.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection, or CBP, is the agency that checks people and goods coming into the country. From October 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026, its officers searched 52,080 electronic devices. That is more than 32 percent higher than the 39,251 searched during the same months a year earlier. It is almost as many as the record 55,424 devices searched in the whole previous year.

Most were basic searches, which an officer can do without suspecting anything wrong. About 4,564 were advanced searches, which are allowed when an officer suspects a law has been broken or there is a security concern. In those, the officer may study or copy what is on the device.

A CBP spokesperson said the searches are "exceedingly rare," affecting only about 0.01 percent of travelers. She said they help find illegal digital material, terrorism-related content and information about whether visitors may enter.

Esha Bhandari of the American Civil Liberties Union, a group that works on privacy rights, said Congress should look more closely at the searches. She said the government does not explain the increase and that it hurts travelers' privacy.

CBP did not say where the searches happened or how many involved U.S. citizens. Laura Dawson, who leads a group focused on border issues, said the rise is hard to judge without those details. She pointed out that many people traveled for the World Cup this summer.

The story raises a question many families may think about: how to balance safety at the border with personal privacy.
why_it_matters: Phones hold a lot of personal information, so the rise in border searches raises a bigger question about how to balance national security with travelers' privacy rights.

background_read: U.S. Customs and Border Protection is the federal agency that checks travelers and goods arriving at airports, seaports and land borders.
Border officers have broad power to inspect what people bring into the country, and today that can include the data stored on phones and laptops.
Privacy groups such as the American Civil Liberties Union argue that phones hold very personal information, so searching them should have clear limits and checks by Congress or the courts.
